item.title: Meta settles with states, sets new industry standards over child safety
item.description:
Meta agreed to settle with U.S. states for up to $16.7 billion in a landmark deal over allegations Facebook and Instagram were designed in ways that harm children.

  • The company is calling on its peers to sign on to the pact as well, saying it won't work unless they jointly line up behind broad reform.

Why it matters: This is social media's version of the landmark 1990s tobacco settlement, a settlement that effectively reshapes the industry and the way young Americans experience some of their favorite platforms.

Driving the news: Meta agreed to provide compensation to the states for a variety of public health purposes, including crisis intervention services, after-school programs, outdoor activities and youth mental health programming.

  • Meta also agreed to limited under-18 users to 2 hours per day on Facebook and Instagram, block them from accessing the platforms from midnight to 6 a.m., and limit notifications to them during school hours.
  • Youth will also be given the option to have a chronological feed, not an algorithmic one — and parents can make it the default option.
  • Kids also won't be able to see likes and other reactions on posts.

The intrigue: Alongside the settlement, Meta issued an open letter to TikTok and YouTube calling on them to join in the deal.

  • "We want to ensure teens benefit from this new industry standard, but we cannot do it alone. These protections will only be truly effective if we work with our peers - TikTok and YouTube - to put the same measures in place," the letter says, per a source to Axios.
  • "All platforms should empower parents and support teens in these ways because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another. For meaningful progress to happen, we urge our peers to join us."

About $5 billion of the Meta settlement kicks in only if YouTube and TikTok also settle with states on two conditions:

  1. Imposing a one-hour daily usage limit, night restrictions, and age assurance features;
  2. Paying about $5 billion each.

By the numbers: Meta shares edged up slightly after the deal.

  • Investors had been bracing for the possibility of a much larger payout if the ongoing trial went to a jury verdict, with penalties ranging up to $1.4 trillion.
  • The company said it expects to take a $10 billion charge in the current quarter for the settlement, which was not part of its prior guidance.

Follow the money: At roughly $17 billion, the Meta settlement is on par with historic federal civil settlements like the Volkswagen "Dieselgate" scandal and the BP Deepwater Horizon deal.

  • But it's a small fraction of the 1998 tobacco deal, under which states collected more than $200 billion.

The other side: "This is not just about money — it's about changing how these platforms operate so they stop exploiting the developing brains of our kids," Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said in a statement.

  • "Indiana will continue working with other states to secure similar protections from companies like Discord, Roblox, Snapchat, TikTok, and YouTube. Our children deserve better, and we will keep fighting until they get it."

What's next: The deal is expected to end the trial with a judge's approval.

This is breaking news. Check back for updates.

item.title: Jeffries faces impeachment dilemma if Democrats win back the House
item.description:
With just 10 weeks left until the midterms, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) gave CNN's Wolf Blitzer a preview yesterday of what to expect should Democrats regain control of the House:

  • "Hold every single member of the Trump cartel accountable."
  • "Make sure that we've got people in government focused on doing the things necessary to address the affordability crisis."
  • On impeachment, "we haven't ruled anything in and we haven't ruled anything out", with any move guided by "moments of accountability."

That aligns with the priorities Jeffries has been pushing on the stump:

  1. Lower the cost of living.
  2. Make health care affordable.
  3. Take the Trump administration to task.

But his careful line on impeachment underscores how he could become Speaker with one wing of his caucus pushing to aggressively confront President Trump while the other is desperate to avoid another impeachment fight.

  • The most pro-impeachment Democrats from Trump's first term have fallen in recent primaries, but that doesn't mean there isn't any momentum behind trying again, lawmakers stressed.
  • "There are plenty of good reasons that Trump should be impeached based on his actions," one senior House Democrat told Axios.

The real question is political. Some Democrats aren't convinced it's worth pursuing again when two prior impeachments failed to stop Trump's return to the White House.

  • "I believe that we will not do impeachment again. It's a major time suck — and will do nothing to forward our agenda," a second senior House Democrat said.
  • That lawmaker added that it "depends if we win the Senate," though Democrats won't get anywhere close to the 67 seats that would be needed to convict Trump in a party-line vote.

Go deeper: Inside the backlash over the Jeffries-Kushner meeting

item.title: Stanley Druckenmiller makes AI writing a billionaire flex
item.description:
Legendary investor Stanley Druckenmiller made AI writing seem like no big deal this week, telling NOTUS reporter Jeff Stein "of course" he used it to help draft a widely shared op-ed for the Wall Street Journal.

Why it matters: The moment could mark a real cultural shift where AI writing is basically all good, at least among a certain set of influential elites.

Where it stands: Among his intended audience in the financial world, Druckenmiller's article got more attention for its substance — a scathing critique of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent — than for its style.

  • The writing is infused with the telltale cadences of the AI-generated one-two punch — for example, "If the 30-year must trade at 5.5% to clear, that isn't a crisis. It is an invoice."
  • Or this familiar construct: "This wasn't liquidity management, it was price management ... "

State of play: Many folks on "fintwits," the finance community on X, formerly known as Twitter, not only seemed willing to overlook the method, but praised it:

  • "Druck using AI to write the op ed is the sickest burn of 2026," Claudia Sahm, a former economist for the Federal Reserve posted. "Didn't even waste his time writing up why Bessent was wrong."

The big picture: The WSJ's opinions section threw open the floodgates to more AI-generated op-eds in its response to the discourse.

  • "AI is a fact of modern life. People will use it to assist in their work and writing, including with research, checking grammar, editing and more," WSJ opinion editor Paul Gigot said in a statement.
  • "The question for us is whether what we publish from contributors reflects an author's original argument, and if the author has the standing and credibility to make it."
  • "In Stan Druckenmiller's case, we have had a relationship with him for many years, and nobody can doubt that his op-ed is his genuine opinion."

Worth noting: The WSJ newsroom, separate from Gigot's team, has a different policy on AI use.

Friction point: The reaction was very different to the response earlier this month when Harvard professor Ricardo Hausmann was criticized for using AI to write a column for the Financial Times.

  • The paper ultimately appended a note at the top: "It has come to our attention that AI was used to condense a longer draft of this column prior to submission to the FT and our own editorial involvement."
  • "The FT editorial code of conduct specifically prohibits the use of AI in the writing process."

Zoom in: Druckenmiller likened using AI to using a calculator.

  • "There's a reason I moved from an English major to being an economics major," Druckenmiller told Stein. "I'm not embarrassed by it ... I write everything using AI now for the same reason I use a calculator when I do math problems."

Between the lines: For the most part, plenty of billionaires already employ ghostwriters to spin up their op-eds, LinkedIn musings and social media posts. Transitioning to AI seems like a natural progression.

Zoom out: For everyone else, it's not clear yet if they can get away with this. Druckenmiller's AI-gate comes in the context of a broader backlash to the intersection of AI and content.

  • YouTuber Hank Green faced backlash after viewers of a video last month accused him of using AI to write his script. He later shared an policy on how he'll use the tech going forward.
  • "Where do you draw the line of what's immoral and what is moral?" content creator and marketing strategist Sam Ogborn told Axios.

Madison Mills contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump's "election integrity" threat: Defunding state and local police
item.description:
State and cities nationwide are rebelling against the White House's push to withhold millions of dollars in police and anti-terrorism funding unless they impose new voting rules.

Why it matters: President Trump's effort to impose election policies that he hasn't been able to get through Congress has now drawn two lawsuits from state and local governments that accuse the administration of threatening to defund the police unless Trump gets his way.

  • "They are trying to defund public safety and counterterrorism," Harris County (Texas) Attorney Abbie Kamin told Axios.
  • Harris County, which includes Houston, and the other jurisdictions stand to lose millions in public safety grants unless they impose the controversial voting rules Trump wants: a plan to transition to paper ballots, proof of citizenship verifications, mandatory hand-counted audits of 5% of all ballots, and more.
  • (A separate part of Trump's "election integrity" push got a boost Monday when the Supreme Court lifted a block on his plan to use the Postal Service to help limit deliveries of mail-in ballots. The plan still faces legal challenges.)

Zoom in: Harris County joined Columbus, Ohio, Nashville, Tenn., and El Paso County, Texas, last week in suing the Department of Homeland Security over the agency's effort to withhold grant money.

  • State and local officials say DHS's demands for costly and unnecessary voting restrictions have put them at risk of losing money for anti-terrorism teams, equipment to counter drone and bomb attacks, protective gear and overtime pay, among other things.
  • "We have dedicated public servants of again all political backgrounds that are involved in ensuring that elections are run securely and fairly," Kamin said.
  • "But what's happening here is the threat to public safety funding and withholding counterterrorism dollars that local law enforcement relies on for partisan political purposes for one individual, and that is Donald Trump."

The other side: In July, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin threatened to withhold federal funding from state governments, echoing Trump's claim that there were thousands of noncitizens on state voter rolls.

  • "I obviously can't force the states" to work with the administration, Mullin said then. But "we are not going to spend taxpayer dollars reimbursing the states that are refusing to secure their elections."
  • "We fully expected opposition to common-sense measures designed to protect election security and safeguard the integrity of American democracy," a FEMA spokesperson said in a statement.
  • "Election security is national security, and protecting our critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump administration."

Zoom out: Besides the lawsuit filed last week, 25 Democrat-lead states filed suit earlier this summer contesting Trump's demands on election procedures.

  • Some Republican-led jurisdictions have expressed a willingness to go along with at least some of the voting changes Trump wants, particularly the use of a federal database to check against voter rolls for citizenship.
  • But for the most part, officials nationwide have said state and local laws already are sufficient to run elections, audit them and maintain voter rolls — work that's constitutionally tasked to state and local governments.
  • "This type of ask ... feeds into this false narrative that our elections are not secure, and that if we do not do these things that the federal government is demanding that local elections are compromised," El Paso County attorney Christina Sanchez. "That is so far from the truth."
  • Just transitioning to paper ballots alone would cost her county $3 million, Sanchez said.

The big picture: Losing the public safety grants would have a huge impact on their jurisdictions, officials said in the lawsuit filed last week.

  • In Texas, Harris and El Paso counties are planning to use the grant funds to buy equipment that can detect hazardous materials and chemicals, explosives and biological weapons.
  • Nashville and Columbus' city governments said they've previously used such funds to buy machines that can detect explosives and purchase SWAT team gear.

Between the lines: This isn't the first time Trump's administration has tried to withhold federal funding from governments that it views as non-compliant with its wishes.

  • Trump has threatened to cut funding to state and local governments that have sanctuary immigration laws preventing local police from collaborating with ICE agents, for example.
  • The administration's threats have failed when challenged in court before.
  • "We've been prepared for this since the beginning of the Trump administration, that they're going to try and play games with cities like Columbus' funding," City Attorney Zach Klein told Axios.
  • "This is the latest example of Trump coming in," he added "It's illegal and it's unconstitutional."

item.title: Inside the backlash over the Jeffries-Kushner meeting
item.description:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries' long-standing tensions with his party's left flank resurfaced this week after news broke of his meeting with President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Why it matters: Jeffries will have to make nice with the left next year if Democrats win back the House with only a narrow majority. Blowups like this are not helping.

  • The Democratic leader defended the meeting in a video posted to social media on Monday, saying that Kushner "asked for a meeting, and I took it, to discuss the affordability crisis."
  • Jeffries (D-N.Y.) suggested Kushner, whose dealings with Saudi Arabia have drawn scrutiny from Democratic congressional investigators, remains a top oversight target.
  • "No one is going to get a pass," he said. "We're going to hold every single member of the Trump cartel accountable, beginning on day one."

What they're saying: The meeting was "definitely a signal about the kind of Speaker Jeffries would be," said Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of the progressive group OurRevolution.

  • The meeting "reinforces the worry from our base that Jeffries' instinct is to negotiate with the Trump power structure rather than draw lines and fight it," he said.
  • Geevarghese and Justice Democrats spokesperson Usamah Andrabi both noted the meeting comes after Jeffries said on Meet the Press that Medicare for All, a central pillar of the left's platform, is "not legislation ... that I support."
  • "Opposing Medicare for All and having secret meetings with Donald Trump's son-in-law sounds more like the leadership of the Republican Party than the fighters Democratic voters are demanding in Congress," Andrabi told Axios.

Jeffries, a onetime co-sponsor of Medicare for All who dropped off the bill when he joined party leadership, said in a later radio interview that health care must "be a right available to every single American."

  • The Democratic leader said there are "different paths" to achieve universal coverage.
  • Those include Medicare for All, he said, but "other folks within the caucus ... think that there are other ways to get there."

What we're hearing: House Democrats and Democratic congressional aides, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer candid thoughts about their party's leader, questioned why Jeffries met with someone who has no official role in the administration.

  • "Of all the people he could meet with, this strikes me as odd," said one lawmaker. "I just wouldn't think Kushner would be the main guy to do that. Strange."
  • Lawmakers and aides also said Jeffries has not issued any private, Democratic caucus-wide explanation for the meeting.

Between the lines: "They have a relationship," a senior House Democrat told Axios of Jeffries and Kushner, noting that they "worked on criminal justice" together during Trump's first term.

  • The meeting was focused on potential areas of common ground between Kushner and the Democratic leader, according to the New York Times, which first reported it.
  • The two discussed housing, immigration and affordability, with Kushner suggesting Jeffries meet with White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, according to a source familiar with the matter.
  • Jeffries said in a CNN interview Tuesday morning: "The American people want us in Washington to solve problems. And I'm not simply here to make a point, but I'm also here to make a difference."

The other side: "The media is trying to make this a big deal, but members are trying to enjoy the last week of August recess. Lots of CODELS and some are working," said the senior House Democrat.

  • One progressive lawmaker told Axios of Jeffries: "People have the common sense that he's the only person who's going to run for Speaker and most of us like him personally."
  • "We deal with him privately rather than publicly ... If everyone knows it's inevitable he's gonna be the Speaker, why would anyone go on record?"

The bottom line: "It's less who you meet with than what you do with the meeting," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.

  • "When Gavin Newsom meets with a right-winger, he concedes points -- while Elizabeth Warren gets Republicans to go along with housing bills and free hearing aids," he said.
  • Green added: "Time will tell what Jeffries does with this."

item.title: Court ruling threatens Republicans' midterm TV ad advantage
item.description:
A federal appeals court ruling Tuesday could erase a new midterm advantage for Republicans.

Why it matters: The 2-1 ruling would block Republicans from using cash-rich party committees to buy more political TV ads at discounted rates.

  • Republicans plan to appeal the decision, setting up another high-stakes campaign finance fight as the fall ad wars heat up ahead of November.

Driving the news: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled the FCC was wrong to extend discounted candidate broadcast rates to political parties and joint fundraising committees that include non-candidate groups for ads they coordinate with candidates.

  • The rates paid by super PACs and other outside groups are often several times higher than candidate rates.
  • The case was brought by four Democratic candidates running this cycle — Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.), former Sen. Sherrod Brown (Ohio), former Gov. Roy Cooper (N.C.) and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (Mich.)
  • The U.S. Supreme Court in June struck down limits on how much committees can spend in coordination with campaigns.

Between the lines: Republicans believed the Supreme Court decision, paired with FCC guidance extending candidate rates to certain coordinated ads, would allow party committee cash to stretch further.

  • The ruling applied to both parties.
  • But while Democratic candidates generally have stronger grassroots fundraising, Republican Party committees have amassed larger war chests, fueled by megadonors
  • Republicans believed the Supreme Court decision, paired with FCC guidance, allowed party committee cash to stretch further by accessing lower rates reserved for candidates.

What they're saying: "Put plainly, today's ruling makes clear that lowest unit rate is an exclusive right given to candidates and incumbent campaigns and that is the law of the land," DSCC executive director Devan Barber and DCCC executive director Julie Merz said in a joint statement.

  • "Democratic candidates' strong grassroots fundraising amplifying the voice of everyday Americans remains a fundamental advantage in the midterms," they continued.
  • "This was an incorrect ruling that ignores decades of precedent," NRSC communications director Joanna Rodriguez said in a statement.
  • "We plan on appealing and this is the first word not the last," she continued.

item.title: Darline Graham wins South Carolina GOP Senate runoff
item.description:
Sen. Darline Graham, President Trump's endorsed candidate, won the Republican nomination Tuesday to fill the Senate vacancy created by her brother Lindsey Graham's death, per the AP.

Why it matters: The victory underscores Trump's continued sway with Republican voters and positions Graham as the odds-on favorite to win a full term in November.

  • Graham, 62, will be heavily favored against Democrat Annie Andrews in November. Democrats have not won a U.S. Senate election in South Carolina since 1998.

Driving the news: Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman finished first and second, respectively, in the Aug. 11 primary and advanced to Tuesday's runoff after neither won the majority needed to secure the nomination outright.

  • Graham entered the race July 20, days after Gov. Henry McMaster (R) appointed her to serve temporarily in the seat held by her late brother — her first time holding elected office.
  • Her abbreviated primary campaign benefited from Trump's endorsement, the advantages of incumbency and one of the most recognizable names in South Carolina politics.
  • In addition to campaigning with Graham in South Carolina on Friday, MAGA Inc. made a last-minute push for her, spending more than $827,000 on phone calls and text messages ahead of Tuesday's vote, according to FEC reports.

Zoom in: Graham's statement during a runoff debate that she was "not that informed on national security," in response to a question about U.S. policy toward Taiwan, fueled questions about her readiness for the job.

  • It also highlighted the contrast with her late brother, who for decades was a Senate leader on foreign policy and national security matters.
  • Norman posted on X: "South Carolina deserves a Senator who UNDERSTANDS Foreign Policy. I'm a PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH supporter! No more forever wars!"

The other side: Norman, 73, argued that Republican voters should judge candidates by their records, presenting himself as a proven conservative rather than a first-time candidate elevated by a famous name.

  • A hard-line conservative, Norman is vice chair of the House Freedom Caucus.
  • In June, Norman placed third in South Carolina's Republican gubernatorial primary, behind Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette and Alan Wilson, the state's attorney general.

Between the lines: Both Graham and Norman flooded the airwaves, spending a combined total of more than $5 million on ads during the primary runoff, according to AdImpact.

  • "Stand with President Trump. Vote Darline Graham for Senate," one pro-Graham ad stated, while another accused Norman of being a "career politician."
  • "This election is not for sale," Norman said in one ad. "South Carolina needs a proven conservative with a record of fighting for you. You shouldn't have to guess where your next senator stands. With me, you already know."

item.title: Rubio tells allies U.S. shifting from strikes to sanctions on Iran
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has told several of his foreign counterparts in recent days that "for the time being" the U.S. is not expected to initiate new strikes against Iran, according to a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter.

  • Instead, he's said the focus is on other means of pressure, including the sanctions initiative announced this week.

Why it matters: Rubio's message to foreign ministers from several allied countries comes as the U.S. believes it's suffocating Iran with the naval blockade — while moving ever-increasing amounts of oil out of the Strait of Hormuz.

  • It's also another sign that President Trump is exasperated with the war and wants it to be over, at least for now.
  • The U.S. official said that while Rubio made clear that the U.S. isn't planning a return to major combat operations, he didn't rule out strikes if Iran attacks first.
  • Another U.S. official said the clearing of mines from the Strait of Hormuz by the U.S. Navy is a watershed moment in the war, largely neutralizing one of Iran's main sources of leverage.

Behind the scenes: The sources said Rubio outlined the Trump administration's current Iran policy in phone calls with several of his counterparts:

  • Avoiding military action against Iran for the time being.
  • Increasing economic pressure on Iran through the U.S. naval blockade and the new Treasury Department sanctions push.
  • Transporting as much oil as possible through the strait and into global energy markets.
  • A second U.S. official said this is expected to be the policy at least until after the midterm elections, when a new military campaign could again be on the table.

State of play: U.S. officials say the clearing of mines from most of the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with the fact that more and more tankers have been moving through the southern lane of the strait in recent weeks, significantly reduces Iran's leverage over global energy markets.

  • "The Iranians have lost control over the strait. Now the U.S. controls it," one U.S. official said.
  • The U.S. naval blockade is depriving Iran of critical revenue. Over the last two weeks, almost no tankers have been spotted at Kharg Island, Iran's main oil export hub, U.S. officials say.
  • "The Iranian economy is in free fall and the regime's military has been decimated," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told Axios, "and we are cutting off every financial lifeline the regime has remaining."
  • He added, "The President has been clear that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, and that he will use the tools necessary to ensure that objective is accomplished."

The big picture: Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, was in Tehran on Sunday for talks with the Iranian leadership. Pakistan has been a key mediator between the U.S. and Iran since the war began.

  • According to Al Arabiya, the Saudi-affiliated TV station, Munir spoke to Trump before the trip and suggested a new proposal for the Iranians.
  • The White House didn't deny that Trump spoke to Munir but said there are no current or scheduled negotiations with Iran.
  • U.S. officials say that the new developments in the strait and the growing volume of oil coming out of the Gulf have deprived Iran of a major card in any future negotiations and made any potential deal between Oman and Iran regarding the strait irrelevant.
  • "Right now we are not negotiating with Iran. We are squeezing them. The pressure could drive the Iranians back to the table," a U.S. official said.

What to watch: White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have been leading the negotiations with Iran, are expected to visit U.S. Central Command on Wednesday for briefings on the situation on the ground, according to a source with knowledge.

item.title: Trump administration violated court order on mail-voting rules, judge says
item.description:
A Massachusetts judge ruled Tuesday that the Trump administration violated a nationwide injunction by finalizing a rule that would significantly overhaul mail voting if allowed to take effect.

Why it matters: The order allows the Trump administration to publish the rule Wednesday, but the U.S. Postal Service remains barred from making the dramatic changes to mail-in ballots.

Driving the news: "Defendants cannot contend that they misunderstood the scope of the court's order, " U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani wrote in a five-page filing Tuesday afternoon.

  • "Accordingly, despite the Defendants' protestations that '[t]he United States takes its obligation to comply with court orders very seriously,' the court finds that Defendants violated the preliminary injunction in this case."

Catch up quick: Tuesday's ruling came in response to a motion from the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts asking Talwani to enforce her nationwide injunction blocking the new mail-ballot rules.

  • The injunction bars the administration from directing USPS to reject ballot mail that doesn't comply with the administration's new design requirements until after the 2026 midterms.
  • It also bars the administration from "initiating or completing rulemaking" to implement the new criteria.

Yes, but: Talwani declined to implement any of the remedies the LWV requested.

Zoom in: The Trump administration argued in an Aug. 25 filing that publishing the new rule did not violate the nationwide injunction because the rule's language specifically says the USPS won't implement the rule while the injunction is in place. Therefore, merely publishing the rule doesn't violate Talwani's order.

  • The administration also insists that the final rule needed an effective date before the midterms so states would have enough time to comply if the injunction were lifted.

Zoom out: The administration also argued that the Supreme Court's ruling Monday in a separate challenge to Trump's mail-voting executive order undercuts Talwani's preliminary injunction.

  • SCOTUS paused a separate injunction Monday, finding the 23 states and D.C. could not challenge the impending policy before the rulemaking process was completed.
  • The justices explicitly said the states could challenge USPS' final rule if it harms them, but found the states lacked standing because any alleged harm hadn't yet happened.
  • The government argues that reasoning means Talwani should not have issued the preliminary injunction and should now vacate it.
  • Talwani did not address the administration's reasoning regarding the Supreme Court's newest order, nor did she decide whether to lift the preliminary injunction.

What we're watching: The coalition of states involved in the Supreme Court case is expected to sue the administration once the final rule is published.

Go deeper: Trump's mail-in voting rules raise fears of federal overreach

item.title: House Democrats' pro-Israel wing gains power on panel overseeing foreign policy
item.description:
A trio of vocally pro-Israel House Democrats were given powerful posts on the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Tuesday, with one taking the reins of the subcommittee that oversees U.S.-Middle East policy.

Why it matters: It is a substantial win for the party's pro-Israel wing despite growing pro-Palestinian sentiment among the party's grassroots.

  • And it could have global ramifications, with Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.) indicating that, if he becomes chair of the Middle East and North Africa subcommittee next year, he will use the position to shore up U.S. support for Israel.
  • "If Democrats take control of the House, I'll be in a position to help steer U.S. policy on Israel and the Middle East," he told Axios.

Driving the news: In addition to Moskowitz leading Democrats on the MENA subcommittee, pro-Israel Reps. Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.) and Wesley Bell (D-Mo.) were appointed to the Foreign Affairs Committee on Tuesday.

  • Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wisc.), a pro-Palestinian progressive and prolific critic of the pro-Israel group AIPAC, was also appointed to the panel.
  • Moskowitz, Wasserman Schultz and Bell all dispatched left-wing primary challengers this election cycle who went after their support of Israel.

What they're saying: Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, said the appointees' "experience, commitment, and expertise will strengthen our work and help guide the committee as it addresses urgent challenges in national security and diplomacy."

  • "I look forward to working closely with all of our members during this turbulent time when Congressional oversight is most needed," added Meeks, who is also a vocal supporter of Israel.

item.title: Kennedy Center's survival depends on Trump, DOJ says in new filing
item.description:
The Trump administration argued in a Monday court filing that the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts must undergo proposed renovations and a cash infusion to survive.

Why it matters: It's the latest in the legal battle over the venue's future, which the administration has proposed to overhaul, including potentially adding President Trump's name to the building.

Driving the news: "An order blocking the Board from appropriately recognizing President Trump," the DOJ argued in Monday's filing, "will cause donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up, and structural rehabilitation to stop."

  • Without Trump's efforts, the filing reads, "the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down."
  • The document also suggests that if the venue deteriorated that way, the Kennedy Center could be replaced with "a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River."
  • Such a venue has "been proposed, by some, for many years," it continued.

Catch up quick: The filing came in response to Rep. Joyce Beatty's (D-Ohio) request for a federal judge to block the Kennedy Center's board from trying once again to put Trump's name on the building.

  • In May, U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper ordered Trump's name removed from the building after its Trump-chaired board, stacked with MAGA allies, voted to rename it "The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts."

Yes, but: Earlier this month, the board pushed forward once again with plans to put the president's name on the center.

  • Cooper said only Congress could change the center's name — but the DOJ argued in Monday's filing that the updated plan would not rename the center.
  • Rather, the board's recent vote approved an inscription under the center's name that would read "renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump," while the physical site would be renamed the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza."

State of play: Internal documents obtained by Axios' Cuneyt Dil demonstrate the scale of Trump's project, which includes $24.7 million to upgrade the Concert Hall, a "Front of the House Renewal" and plumbing and elevator refurbishments.

  • Still, as the administration casts Trump as the Kennedy Center's savior, the Washington Post reported Tuesday that ticket sales and fundraising fell after it adopted Trump's name.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: AI is making critical infrastructure easier to attack
item.description:
Years of warnings about the digital vulnerabilities lurking inside basic utilities are colliding with a new reality: AI is making those weaknesses easier for hackers to exploit.

Why it matters: AI is lowering the barrier for state-backed hackers looking to disrupt or manipulate water systems, power plants and other critical infrastructure.

Driving the news: A recent wave of cyberattacks targeting critical infrastructure is raising new questions about the preparedness of U.S. water systems and a British power plant.

  • The Telegraph reported that Iran-backed hackers broke into a U.K. power plant, prompting a four-day shutdown around the time a series of cyberattacks on U.S. water systems began.
  • U.S. officials warned last week that hackers were actively using an AI-generated exploitation script to target a device commonly found in critical infrastructure that has played a key role in the ongoing attacks on U.S. water systems.
  • Markus Mueller, field CISO at critical infrastructure security firm Nozomi Networks, told Axios he has medium confidence that the U.S. and U.K. attacks are linked to the same threat actor.

The big picture: Policymakers have been warning for years that weak cybersecurity across critical infrastructure could eventually have real-world consequences.

  • Five years ago, Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) warned Congress that cyber weaknesses across U.S. water utilities represented "an extremely dangerous situation."
  • "We're the most wired country in the world. That's good," he told lawmakers. "But we're also the most vulnerable country in the world."

Between the lines: AI isn't fundamentally changing how hackers break into these systems. It's reducing the time and expertise needed to understand specialized equipment and exploit weaknesses that already exist, experts told Axios.

  • Suspected Iranian hackers have long studied U.S. critical infrastructure, including how specialized devices such as programmable logic controllers work.
  • Historically, threat actors might have needed to obtain the devices themselves or pore over technical manuals before they could successfully target them, Mueller said.
  • Now, AI is lowering the "time, cost, and expertise needed to take advantage of weaknesses that already exist," Diana Kelley, chief information security officer at Noma Security, told Axios.

Reality check: Governments haven't simply ignored the problem. But efforts to impose stronger security requirements have moved slowly and repeatedly run into legal, political and funding hurdles.

  • The Environmental Protection Agency attempted during the Biden administration to require water utilities to implement basic cybersecurity measures, but it later rescinded the policy after legal challenges from states and industry groups.
  • Recent federal cuts to cybersecurity resources and uncertainty around federal grant funding for state and local governments "leaves communities more vulnerable to future cyberattacks," Mayuresh Dani, a security research manager at Qualys, told Axios.
  • Cyber hygiene guidance and government advisories alone won't keep pace with attackers, John Gallagher, vice president at automated cybersecurity firm Viakoo, told Axios.
  • "Adversaries will always have an upper hand because of speed when cyber defense relies on bureaucratic budget cycles and multiyear legislative processes," Gallagher said.

Yes, but: So far, the recent attacks appear to have caused only limited disruptions.

  • In some towns, hackers affected the pressure levels for local water supplies and officials issued precautionary boil-water advisories.
  • The Telegraph reported that the cyberattack on the local power plant "had no impact on the U.K.'s wider power supply or energy generation. "

The intrigue: Critical infrastructure remains an alluring target for nation-state hackers precisely because even relatively small disruptions can have highly visible consequences, Margaret Cunningham, vice president of security and AI strategy at Darktrace, told Axios.

  • "AI gives attackers more speed and reach, but it doesn't erase the problems critical infrastructure organizations have been dealing with for years, including exposed operational technology, difficulty patching and systems that cannot simply be switched off," she said.

What to watch: Key details about the U.K. incident remain unknown, including what type of power plant was targeted and which devices the hackers accessed, Mueller said.

Go deeper: AI cyber threats give security leaders decision fatigue

item.title: Ghislaine Maxwell's bid to overturn conviction rejected
item.description:
A federal judge rejected Ghislaine Maxwell's bid to overturn her conviction, finding her claims — including arguments based on newly released Epstein files — were frivolous.

Why it matters: The blistering opinion says the evidence of Maxwell's guilt is "overwhelming" and new evidence hurt more than helped her.

What they're saying: "Maxwell's claims are all meritless and all or almost all are frivolous," U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer wrote in a 67-page opinion.

  • "The vast majority are procedurally barred — either because Maxwell made and lost the same arguments on direct appeal, or because she could have made such arguments on appeal but elected not to do so."
  • "And the purported 'new' evidence to which Maxwell points, principally materials released under the [Epstein Files Transparency Act,] is largely irrelevant to the charges against Maxwell and does not support her claims of error."
  • "On the contrary, to the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings Maxwell challenges."

Catch up quick: Maxwell was convicted of sex trafficking in December 2021.

  • Engelmayer wrote that the government proved she had been "instrumental in an approximately decade-long scheme with Epstein to entice, groom, transport, and traffic numerous young women and underage girls to engage in sexual activity with Epstein."
  • The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld her conviction, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear her appeal last October.

Zoom out: Maxwell is trying to overturn her 20-year sentence, making 10 claims of constitutional and legal errors at her trial and sentencing.

  • Engelmayer rejected every claim and denied Maxwell's request for an evidentiary hearing, writing that there is "no fact that Maxwell fairly puts in dispute that has any potential to disturb the outcome of her trial."
  • An attorney who formerly represented Maxwell did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Trump: Mines fully removed from Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
The U.S. Navy has cleared all mines from the main shipping lane of the Strait of Hormuz, President Trump said on Tuesday.

Why it matters: The clearing, part of a low-key operation the last several months, will allow significantly more oil tankers to transit the strait.

  • The removal of mines reduces Iran's leverage over global energy markets as well as in any future negotiations with the Trump administration.
  • It also makes the draft agreement that Iran and Oman have been negotiating for months far less relevant.

What he's saying: "I have just been informed by the United States Navy that all mines have been removed and/or detonated from within the International Waters of the Strait of Hormuz," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • Trump added that Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be "immediately and systematically destroyed."
  • He said the U.S. Space Force is closely monitoring the strait. "There is a Zero Tolerance policy on mine placement in full force and effect," Trump wrote.

Behind the scenes: Two U.S. officials with direct knowledge of the matter confirmed Trump's announcement and said the U.S. Navy has cleared the Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) — the median lane of the strait that is right between Oman and Iran.

  • Iran deployed dozens of mines in the median lane during the war, creating a huge danger for ships. It committed to remove the mines as part of the memorandum of understanding reached over the summer with the U.S. But the MOU unraveled and the mines were never removed.
  • Over the last several months, U.S. Navy underwater drones systematically scanned the area and located more than 100 objects that were suspected to be mines.
  • The U.S. military contracted with private companies to remove or detonate the mines.

State of play: The clearing of the median lane in the Strait of Hormuz comes as the U.S. military has been using the southern lane close to the coast of Oman to move oil tankers in and out of the Gulf.

  • U.S. officials say that in the last 30 days, more than 500 ships went in and out of the strait through the southern channel, with only around 2% of those hit by Iranian drones or missiles.
  • Now that the mines have been cleared, ships will be able to move simultaneously in both directions through the strait with protection from the U.S. Air Force, allowing the export of more oil to global energy markets.

The big picture: Trump's announcement came as the foreign ministers of Iran and Oman were meeting in Tehran to negotiate an agreement for navigating the strait. They did not reach a deal.

  • In a joint statement, Iran and Oman said they're discussing a framework to create a temporary joint corridor through the strait and clear mines, while holding technical talks on a permanent navigation route and the future administration of the Strait.
  • The two countries are also discussing a "mechanism for information exchange, traffic management, and the provision of relevant maritime and security services."
  • Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi said after the meeting that he hopes Iran and Oman "will soon announce a temporary corridor for the Strait of Hormuz and practical arrangements to restore safe navigation."

Yes, but: It's unclear whether an Omani-Iranian agreement would be relevant.

  • The U.S. blockade is stopping Iranian ships from moving through the strait. And Trump's announcement today on mine removal — coupled with the fact that more and more tankers have been moving through the southern lane of the strait in recent weeks — means the U.S. is already getting much of what it wants in the strait.

item.title: CIA director Ratcliffe visits Moscow
item.description:
CIA director John Ratcliffe is visiting Moscow on Tuesday for talks with Russian officials, two U.S. officials said.

Why it matters: This is Ratcliffe's first trip to Moscow since he took office and the highest-level visit by a Trump administration official to Russia since January.

  • Ahead of Ratcliffe's trip, the U.S. told Ukraine that a senior delegation was traveling to Moscow and asked it to suspend strikes until it leaves, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.

  • On Tuesday, Ratcliffe travelled from Riga, Latvia to Moscow on a U.S. Air Force C-17 plane.

item.title: "Lake America": Trump turns Canada feud toward Lake Ontario
item.description:
President Trump's war of words with Canada continued Tuesday amid a dispute over trade negotiations.

The big picture: U.S. and Canadian officials have swapped barbs since negotiations collapsed last week, but Trump took the spat to a new level when he threatened to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America" and claimed Canada had lied about a sticking point in trade talks.

What they're saying: "The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don't expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer." Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • Lake Ontario stretches across the U.S.-Canada border, with approximately 47% of the lake belonging to the U.S. Later in the morning, Trump posted a map of the lake, with "Lake Ontario" crossed out and "Lake America" in gold letters above it.
  • The president then posted that he would "never interfere with Canadians speaking French!" referencing comments Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made about U.S. threats to the French language.
  • "In fact, I have never even thought of doing such a stupid thing," Trump added. Carney's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Catch up quick: U.S.-Canada trade talks collapsed Friday night, triggering 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods. Carney said he would match those levies dollar-for-dollar.

  • And on Monday, Trump upped his threats, saying the U.S. will raise car and truck tariffs to 50%, though the duties won't take effect until 2027.
  • The president had previously signaled a deal with Canada was coming, but both sides blamed the other for the talks crumbling.

Zoom out: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer also told CNBC that alleged threats to the French language were a "funny fake story."

  • But he alluded to one pain point: Hotly contested Canadian mandates compelling streaming companies to promote and invest in Canadian content that have long been in flux.

What we're watching: Carney said Monday that "of course" Canada will come back to the negotiating table — if the U.S. has the "right attitude."

Go deeper: Mark Carney's defiance of Trump has Canada cheering

item.title: Exclusive: Climate group presses Dems to seize on data center backlash
item.description:
A climate group that backs Democrats is giving the party's 2028 hopefuls and campaign committees advice on how to capitalize on waning public support for data centers, a new memo shows.

Why it matters: Data centers have landed atop the political radar, and Climate Power's memo underscores the scramble to turn the backlash into a political advantage ahead of the midterms and 2028.

Driving the news: It says "public opinion on data centers is cratering" and argues this provides a political opening around energy costs and environmental concerns.

  • The "topline message" is that "Trump and Republicans have given AI data centers a blank check to raise our utility bills, poison our air, and drain our water," Climate Power argues.

State of play: Democrats can draw a contrast with President Trump's AI and data center advocacy by uniting around three principles, it states.

  • Tech companies paying their own way.
  • Powering data centers with clean energy.
  • Giving communities a "real say" and ensuring they're informed about water and energy usage.

Reality check: Candidates' positions on data centers don't split along partisan lines as various GOP candidates and leaders offer new restrictions.

  • Demands that tech companies and developers don't offload costs onto consumers are common in both parties — and the White House has the same position.
  • And Democrats don't have a united front, with high-profile incumbents and candidates taking a variety of approaches.

Yes, but: Jesse Lee, a senior adviser to Climate Power, argues that Republicans are politically saddled with President Trump's overall support for the sector and will bend to his goals.

  • The memo says that while some GOP candidates are now emphasizing data center accountability, "Trump owns the party's position."

If Republicans keep control of the House and Senate, GOP lawmakers will be an "army for data centers" on Trump's behalf, Lee said in an interview.

  • He also said that while Democrats have room to debate specific policies, they're broadly united around the memo's principles.
  • The memo says that debate could include whether to pursue "real, enforced guardrails" or a temporary moratorium on data centers.

What we're watching: Data center politics are evolving quickly as the midterms loom and Democrats jockey for position ahead of 2028.

  • Climate Power said it shared the memo with the Democratic National Committee, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, and the Democratic Governors Association.
  • The group declined to offer a list of potential 2028 hopefuls who got it, though Lee said it's "pretty much everybody that has been in the conversation."

item.title: Trump's Iran "D-Day" leaves sanctions hammer hanging
item.description:
President Trump's "economic D-Day" for Iran came and went Monday with little of the shock or awe it promised, amounting instead to yet another extended ultimatum.

Why it matters: Operation Economic Outcast will unfold not like the Allied invasion of Normandy, but as a sweeping, slow-burn sanctions campaign that could eventually lock Iran's foreign enablers out of the U.S. financial system.

Zoom in: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent kicked off the operation by blacklisting more than 60 Iran-linked targets and widening the reach of secondary sanctions. "Every country has a defined timeline to shut down activities we have identified," he said.

  • Bessent declined to name specific countries or deadlines, saying the administration preferred "quiet diplomacy" before resorting to "the hammer of U.S. Treasury actions."
  • "Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?" he told reporters when pressed on the gradual rollout, saying countries deserve a chance to change their behavior.

Between the lines: The real test will be China, which accounts for roughly 90% of Iran's exported oil and remains one of the regime's most important economic lifelines.

  • If Trump follows through on his threats, secondary sanctions could force Chinese banks, refiners and shippers to choose between Iran and access to dollars, U.S. banks and markets.
  • Asked specifically whether China would be targeted, Bessent insisted that "no one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions." But he gave no public indication of when the clock runs out — or what Trump is prepared to do if Beijing refuses to play ball.

The intrigue: Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to visit the White House on Sept. 24, giving Trump another reason to think twice before risking a new confrontation with the world's second-largest economy.

The big picture: After months of apocalyptic threats to bomb Iran into submission, Trump has turned to economic strangulation as his preferred strategy through the midterms.

  • The pivot has obvious political advantages: sanctions and a naval blockade can keep squeezing Tehran without immediately risking another oil shock or deeper entanglement in an unpopular war.
  • But economic coercion depends heavily on credibility. China, Dubai and other remaining gateways to Iran have to believe Trump will eventually impose the enormous costs he's threatening if they refuse to cooperate.

The bottom line: The U.S. already has powerful secondary sanctions on the books, but has enforced them only selectively.

  • Operation Economic Outcast will be judged by whether Trump is willing to use them against the countries that matter most.
  • "By now the world will have to see it to believe it," warned the Wall Street Journal editorial board, pointing to six months of threats, shifting deadlines and predictions of imminent victory.

item.title: Mark Carney's defiance of Trump has Canada cheering
item.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has turned his decision to hold firm against President Trump's tariff threats into a rallying point for Canadians as their trade clash escalates.

Why it matters: The mild-mannered former Bank of Canada and Bank of England governor is holding firm against Trump despite the threat of further economic pain for Canadians.

Context: Carney campaigned on standing up to Trump but has generally dealt with the unpredictable U.S. president with the measured temperament of his central banking days.

  • That combination of restraint and resolve has made Carney Canada's "man for the moment," Andrea Lawlor, an associate professor of political science at McMaster University in Ontario, tells Axios.

Driving the news: Carney walked away from trade talks with the Trump administration Friday and vowed to match new 50% U.S. tariffs "dollar for dollar," winning broad support at home.

  • Corpay chief market strategist Karl Schamotta said Monday that Carney appears to be betting that November's midterms will blunt Trump's tariff drive, "opening the way to a mutually beneficial deal."

State of play: Lawlor notes Carney has enjoyed a "very extended political honeymoon" since his long-governing Liberal Party was re-elected last year.

  • Carney was already popular before his latest clash with Trump. His approval rating rose 3 points to 60% last week, while a poll conducted during the same period showed most Canadians wanted a tougher approach to U.S. trade talks, days before the talks collapsed.
  • He has also won broad support from provincial premiers across party lines, including Ontario conservative Doug Ford, who has aggressively pushed back against Trump's tariff threats, and Manitoba social democrat Wab Kinew, who said he's "100%" behind Carney.

Threat level: Carney is under pressure to deliver on his promise that Canadians "are already giving ourselves more than they can take away."

  • He'll have to show how Canada can "give more to ourselves," Lawlor says, including through major projects that create jobs for people facing less stable employment prospects.
  • The risk for Carney is that economic pain could test that support. Canada's unemployment rate is already 6.4%, and Lawlor says it could rise if the trade fight drives more steel and auto manufacturing out of industrial hubs such as southwestern Ontario.
Screenshot: Ontario Premier Doug Ford/X

Between the lines: It's not all about Carney. Trump's continued threats over tariffs and to make Canada the "51st state" have generated a powerful anti-Trump response among Canadians.

  • The trade standoff has become a matter of sovereignty, not merely tariffs.
  • Carney's central banking background, however, gives him "a skill set of handling extraordinarily difficult situations" requiring responses that are "economically sound and fiscally prudent," Lawlor says.
  • His combination of knowledge and temperament makes him "a really well-suited figure for this moment," she adds.

Zoom out: Canada's refusal to accept Trump's terms contrasts with other major U.S. trading partners that have made concessions to avert steeper tariffs, like the EU.

  • Consulting firm Kearney's Drew DeLong says Canada is testing whether "greater strategic autonomy is worth increased trade friction."
  • That test is becoming starker. Trump on Monday told Canada to "fall in line," while Carney said Canada would not accept being treated as a "subsidiary of the United States."

What we're watching: Lawlor says Canadians have little choice but to continue backing Carney's stance, even if the dispute drags on, because Trump's proposed terms are "patently unfair and not sustainable" for Canadian industry.

  • Canada is beginning a long-term effort to shift some of its trade away from the U.S., bringing "short, medium, and long-term pain," she says.

Go deeper: Escalated U.S.-Canada trade talks threaten fallout

item.title: Supreme Court upholds Trump's order to overhaul mail-in ballots
item.description:
President Trump can implement an executive order restricting mail-in ballots just months before the midterm elections, the Supreme Court said Monday.

Why it matters: It's a win for the president, who has opposed mail-in voting for years, but the legal battle is far from over, and the exact impact on November's elections is still unclear.

Driving the news: The Supreme Court said in the unsigned order that states lack standing to challenge the executive order because it was an "internal directive" that didn't harm the states that sued. But the majority wrote that the administration was "likely to suffer irreparable harm" from the freeze.

  • "This internal directive does not regulate the States' voter registration processes," the court's order reads. "Nor does it impinge on the States' authority 'to create and enforce a legal code' for elections."
  • A federal appeals court previously found the order could impose "unprecedented levels of involvement by federal officials in how states administer elections" and could confuse and disenfranchise voters.
  • "The Court's disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful, the court noted. "On that score, time will tell."

The other side: The court's three liberal justices — Ketanji Brown Jackson, Sonya Sotomayor and Elena Kagan — dissented.

  • The decision did not address whether the administration has the authority to implement Trump's order, Sotomayor noted in her dissent, which Kagan joined. Rather, they argued, "today's decision merely postpones adjudication of those challenges."
  • Jackson echoed them, saying the court had "not foreclosed States from challenging this blatantly unconstitutional Order. But it declines to explain when, exactly, is the right time to bring a meritorious election-rule claim challenging unconstitutional interference with electoral processes."

Catch up quick: Trump's executive order, issued in March of this year, directed the Department of Homeland Security to compile a list of citizens eligible to vote and called for the U.S. Postal Service to accept ballots only from voters on those lists.

  • Eligible voter rolls constantly change as people move, die, turn 18 or change their names. A national list would quickly become outdated, according to voting rights groups.
  • A coalition of Democratic state attorneys general challenged the order.
  • In June, Judge Indira Talwani of Massachusetts blocked key parts of his order. A federal appeals court upheld the order in July, leading the administration to turn to the Supreme Court.

Yes, but: This month, Talwani also issued a separate, broader ruling blocking the president's attempted nationwide voting overhaul.

  • Election Day is less than three months away, and today's order does not end the legal battle. All eyes will now likely turn to Talwani's nationwide injunction and what the Supreme Court will decide in that case.

Between the lines: Under the Constitution, states — not the president — administer elections.

  • Congress does have the authority to pass legislation that alters election rules.
  • Government reports and voting rights groups have consistently found voter fraud is rare and, when it occurs, is not widespread enough to affect election outcomes.

What we're watching: Trump has repeatedly pressured Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would impose stricter voting rules.

  • The bill would not end mail-in voting and faces an uphill climb in Congress. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has repeatedly said it lacks the support to pass.

Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

Go deeper: Thune's shield against Trump

item.title: America's elections are getting caught in a fight over the mail
item.description:
President Trump's push to restrict mail-in voting through the U.S. Postal Service could allow the federal government to exert control over voting data and state-run elections, voting rights groups say.

Why it matters: Questions remain about what will happen with mail-in voting this election cycle. On Monday, the Supreme Court cleared one roadblock for Trump's push to restrict mail-in ballots via the U.S. Postal Service, but a separate nationwide injunction keeps the rule blocked for now.

  • The administration's proposed rule for mail-in ballots could scramble the 2026 midterms by forcing local and state officials to adopt an untested federal system on short notice and potentially undermine confidence in U.S. elections.
  • The policy would require USPS to review outgoing mail-ballot envelopes for compliance with federal requirements before accepting them.
  • Election officials would also have to use a new Federal Ballot Mail Portal to submit personal information about voters receiving mail ballots.

Driving the news: The Supreme Court's Monday decision overturned a lower-court ruling blocking a suit from 23 states and D.C. over the president's executive order, which created a citizenship-list system and changed mail-ballot rules.

  • The court ruled that the coalition of states had sued the administration too early. SCOTUS found the lawsuit invalid because the states lacked standing to challenge the executive order, which they said imposed no obligations on the states.

The intrigue: Monday's ruling is "certainly not the end of this story," Jonathan Diaz, director of voting advocacy and partnerships at the Campaign Legal Center, tells Axios.

  • "This is not the Supreme Court saying yes, 'this order is legal and constitutional, and you definitely can do this by November.' This was really just a technical ruling about the timing of the district court's order."
  • He added that the states are still free to sue the administration once the rule is published in the federal register, which is scheduled for August 26.

Catch up quick: The League of Women Voters of Massachusetts filed a separate motion Saturday seeking to enforce a federal court order blocking USPS from implementing the rules.

  • That suit is one of several seeking to block the rules from taking effect. A third Massachusetts case blocks USPS nationwide from enforcing the mail-ballot rules for Nov. 3. Voting rights groups say USPS violated that order by finalizing the rules anyway.
  • Two D.C. cases have gone more favorably for the administration but don't erase the nationwide block.

What they're saying: "It would be, I think, functionally impossible for some places to comply with these rules," Diaz says.

  • He said the policy could prevent eligible voters from receiving ballots and prove "catastrophic for election administration and for voters."

The other side: White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Axios in an emailed statement that the "real 'chaos' in our elections is sowed by extreme Democrats who refuse to enact basic commonsense measures that ensure Americans, and Americans only, decide our elections."

  • USPS declined to comment because of "pending litigation."

Threat level: The rule would disproportionately harm Americans who rely on mail ballots, including the elderly, voters with disabilities, rural residents, college students, and people working multiple shifts, Diaz says.

  • Voters dealing with sudden illness, travel, or hospitalization could also face delays.

Yes, but: Despite Trump's repeated claims that mail-in voting is unsafe, he has voted by mail multiple times, including earlier this month.

  • States already use safeguards such as signature matching, witness requirements and ID checks to detect fraud, which remains rare.

Between the lines: Trump's attacks on mail voting could also further undermine public confidence in elections.

  • "[H]is rhetoric and then actions like this are solutions in search of a problem," Chris Diaz, director of legislative tracking at the non-partisan Voting Rights Lab says, adding that the president has no authority over elections.
  • "It's just totally unprecedented for the federal government to be trying to impose a top-down solution... This is just attempting to put a level of federal bureaucracy into a state system that's already working."

What we're watching: Whether the DOJ attempts to use Monday's ruling to get other injunctions lifted.

Go deeper: Trump's mail-in voting restrictions blocked nationwide by federal judge

item.title: 5 ways Iran's economy is wilting under Trump's pressure
item.description:
President Trump is escalating economic pressure on Tehran more than six months into the Iran war, aiming to squeeze Iranian leaders into submission.

Why it matters: Trump's campaign could test how much economic pain Iran is willing to take before its leaders tap out.

Driving the news: Trump declared last week that Iran would face an "economic D-Day" amid the ongoing war. The president has been adamant that Iran's economy is "COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!"

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled a plan Monday to cripple Iran's economy in what he called the "single greatest financial offensive ever."

State of play: Iran previously raised significant revenue from oil exports transported through Hormuz. But that source of income was severely curtailed by the U.S. blockade that began in April.

  • Iran is now relying on domestic taxes, non-oil exports and pre-war oil revenue to fund war efforts.
  • Though it's shown no signs of surrender, some Iranian officials have said the country should look to end the war rather than try to endure months or years of economic strain.
  • Some experts believe Iran may lash out militarily before conceding. "Just because the U.S. has decided to pause its full-blown military operation doesn't mean Iran will follow suit," Chris Kennedy, the economic statecraft lead at Bloomberg Economics, told Bloomberg.

What they're saying: Experts say Iran could face severe economic hardship within months that could damage its war efforts and threaten domestic stability.

  • "Iran's financial lifeline has been cut by the U.S. blockade," William Jackson, a chief emerging markets economist at Capital Economics, wrote on Monday.
  • Jackson suggested the big question is how much "economic pain" Iran is "willing to bear to achieve its military and geopolitical objectives."

Here's how Trump's economic headlock is affecting Iran's economy:

Iran's currency is crashing

Zoom in: The country's main form of currency, the rial, fell to 2.02 million per dollar Monday, per the Associated Press, largely due to the economic toll of the war.

  • The rial was worth 1.65 million per dollar just before the war (a record low at the time).
  • This means it now takes 22% more rials to buy one dollar.
A man counts Iranian rial notes while buying gold coins at a store in Tehran on Jan. 28. Photo: Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty Images

Inflation is devouring paychecks

By the numbers: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimated in June that Iran's inflation will hit 68.9% in 2026, the highest figure since 1979, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

  • Iran's own Statistical Centre reported that July consumer prices rose 87.9% compared to last year, with food and beverage inflation alone jumping more than 128%.
  • The report attributed the jump to economic sanctions and regional conflicts.

Iranians are facing financial hardships

What they're saying: The devalued rial and high inflation are making it harder for Iranians to afford basic needs.

  • Ahmad Karimi, a taxi driver, told AP: "We're cutting out fruit, we're cutting out protein, we've given up leisure, we even work on weekends."
  • Iranians, already hurting from the country's economic downturn, have recently been posting grievances on social media.
People browse shops at the Grand Bazaar in Tehran on Aug. 24. Photo: AFP via Getty Images

Oil exports have collapsed

The big picture: Iran's economic crisis stems largely from the collapse in oil exports caused by the blockade.

  • Iran Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said in August the country, like others in the region, is essentially no longer exporting oil.

Flashback: Axios in May reported the U.S. blockade had cost Iran at least $4.8 billion, and its oil reserves have plummeted.

The latest: China, normally a major buyer of Iranian oil, said Monday that it is closely monitoring the situation, with a desire to avoid escalation.

Jobs are disappearing as recession fears rise

Before the war, Iran's economy was expected to grow by 1.1% in 2026, according to the IMF.

  • Iran's GDP is now expected to shrink by 5.4% this year, per the IMF's July forecast.

The forecast switch came amid rising unemployment, disappearing jobs, and declining business activity, fueling fears of recession.

Pressure mounts to concede

What's next: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said last week it might be better for Iran to "end the war today while we are in a position of strength and dignity" as the country endures economic pressure.

Yes, but: There's little evidence Tehran is close to capitulating, according to an analysis from the Institute for the Study of War and The Critical Threats Project at the American Enterprise Institute.

  • Iranian officials blame the U.S. for the failure of the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) last month. That makes them believe any concession won't provide economic relief, the analysis says.
  • "Regime decisionmaking may therefore take a long time to react to economic deterioration, even as the economy gets much worse," per the analysis.

The bottom line: Trump wants to crush Iran with punishing sanctions. But the country has shown before it has a high tolerance for economic pain.

Go deeper: 5 scenarios for how the Iran war could end

item.title: Trump administration to revoke up to 200,000 visas of asylum seekers
item.description:
The Trump administration plans to revoke up to 200,000 business and tourism visas held by people who've sought asylum in the U.S., AP first reported on Monday.

Why it matters: It would be the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history and would likely trigger legal challenges.

What they're saying: "We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told AP.

  • He wouldn't say how many visas might be revoked, adding, "as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."
  • Representatives for the State Department and the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

The big picture: President Trump has made immigration enforcement a key priority during his second administration, aggressively cracking down on undocumented immigrants and revoking visas over issues ranging from pro-Palestinian activism to comments about Charlie Kirk's killing.

  • Last year, the administration began "continuous vetting" of more than 55 million U.S. visa holders for potential violations that could lead to revocation or deportation.

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story. Please check back for updates.

item.title: Flock cameras join data centers as a top AI boogeyman in 2026 midterms
item.description:
Flock cameras are joining data centers as a top midterm boogeyman, with members of Congress and congressional candidates trying to harness a sudden groundswell of grassroots anger over the AI surveillance tool.

Why it matters: This blowup over the country's massive network of license plate readers illustrates how rapidly AI has moved from a peripheral issue in national politics toward the center of the midterm campaign.

  • Data centers have become a major issue in the midterms, with candidates racing to one-up each other in their opposition to building the energy-hungry facilities.
  • Super PACs affiliated with AI companies have also spent tens of millions of dollars clashing with each other in congressional elections over the degree to which the federal government should regulate the technology.
  • Now, surveillance cameras are opening a new front in the debate over AI.

Driving the news: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, posted a video to X Wednesday tying his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, to Flock cameras.

  • "There's been this mass proliferation of Flock cameras, any and everywhere, watching your every move to collect information without you even noticing," El-Sayed says with the '80s tune "Somebody's Watching Me" playing in the background.
  • El-Sayed accuses Rogers of supporting the practice, citing a 2013 hearing in which the then-House Intelligence Committee chair said: "You can't have your privacy violated if you don't know your privacy is violated, right?"
  • The Rogers campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Catch up quick: Flock and similar companies are facing a public outcry over their AI-powered license plate reader cameras, particularly given reports of police officers misusing the technology, Axios reported.

  • Municipalities across the country have already moved to sever ties with Flock — whose vast network of 120,000 cameras allows law enforcement to track the movement of vehicles — and some people have sabotaged the cameras.
  • The company has defended its practices and said it is improving its privacy features, telling Axios it has been "listening to customers, communities, and civil liberties groups."
  • Flock has also argued that the tool is being used for good, saying its cameras have aided roughly 1 million police investigations and helped find around 10,000 missing people.

State of play: Democratic House candidates are getting in on the Flock camera blowback.

  • Ohio Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker said in a statement that her opponent, former House Intelligence Committee Chair Mike Turner (R-Ohio), "pushed for more Flock cameras in downtown Dayton."
  • "Now those cameras have been caught running thousands of searches that broke our city's rules," she added.
  • Turner said in a statement to Axios: "My yellow springs socialist opponent once again shows her ignorance, since the Local Congressman has nothing to do with the number of flock cameras in Dayton, OH."

Chaz Molder, the Democratic nominee in Tennessee's 5th District, said of Flock cameras: "That kind of big government overreach has no place in our country or Tennessee."

  • "Politicians are cashing their checks while allowing their cameras to go up everywhere," said William Lawrence, a progressive Democratic House candidate in Michigan.

Between the lines: Flock cameras are emerging as a rare area of bipartisan agreement on Capitol Hill, with conservatives and progressives in particular speaking out on the issue in recent weeks.

  • A trio of House Republicans led by Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) introduced a bill last month to prohibit the federal government from purchasing Flock cameras or similar technology.
  • Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) wrote in a social media post Tuesday: "Flock has installed nearly 100,000 cameras across America to track your every movement. ... STOP AI MASS SURVEILLANCE. STOP FLOCK."

The bottom line: The Flock camera backlash is converging with the already prominent data center discourse to make AI one of the most potent issues on the campaign trail.

  • Jake Johnson, a Democratic House candidate in Minnesota, told Axios he was not surprised to find voters chafing at Flock cameras given the intense feelings he has encountered about data centers.
  • "Everywhere I go I get questions about data centers," he said. "So the fact that those two are potentially linked together, I think, really, really burns people."
